A.explanation: Too small by almost a factor of 2. $v = 4.1 \times 10^{6} \text{ m s}^{-1}$ gives only about $5.6 \times 10^{-14} \text{ J}$ with the alpha mass.

B.explanation: Obtained if the factor $1/2$ is omitted by using $E_k = mv^2$, so $v = \sqrt{E_k/m} \approx 5.8 \times 10^{6} \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

C.explanation: Correctly uses $v = \sqrt{2E_k/m}$ with $E_k = 2.2 \times 10^{-13} \text{ J}$ and $m \approx 6.6 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$ to give $\approx 8.1 \times 10^{6} \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

D.explanation: Too large by $\sqrt{2}$. It results from using about half the alpha mass, about $3.3 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$, in $v = \sqrt{2E_k/m}$.

hints: Notice the particle is an alpha-particle, which is 2 protons plus 2 neutrons, so its mass is about $4u \approx 6.6 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$, not a single proton mass.
Connect the given $2.2 \times 10^{-13} \text{ J}$ of kinetic energy to speed with $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$, so you need $v = \sqrt{2E_k/m}$.
Substitute $2 \times 2.2 \times 10^{-13} \text{ J}$ divided by $6.6 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$ and take the square root, then check the power of 10 is near $10^6 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough: Recall what is given: kinetic energy $E_k = 2.2 \times 10^{-13} \text{ J}$ and the particle is an alpha-particle.
Recall the alpha-particle mass: 4 nucleons, so $m \approx 4 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg} \approx 6.6 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$.
State the kinetic energy rule: $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$, so rearranged for speed $v = \sqrt{2E_k/m}$.
Check units: $\text{J kg}^{-1} = \text{m}^2 \text{ s}^{-2}$, so the square root is in $\text{m s}^{-1}$, as required. This is option C.
